A table has only two directions and both of them are ordinary, which is why a table is easier to read than most people expect on first meeting one.

  • A row is one of the things the table is about — one loan, one learner, one payment, recorded once, with a value in every column that applies to it.
  • A column is one kind of fact — every value in it means the same thing and is the same kind of thing, which is exactly what makes it possible to filter on it, sort by it, or total it.
  • A key is the column that identifies the row — a value no two rows may share, so that one record can be referred to from elsewhere with no ambiguity about which one is meant.
  • A relationship is a column that names a row in another table — a loan carries a learner identifier rather than a learner’s name, so the name is stored once and borrowed by every loan that needs it.

That last one is the move the files could not make. Correct a name on the learner’s own row and every loan is correct the same instant, because no loan ever held a copy of it in the first place.

Asking a table something is then three separate decisions, and keeping them separate is most of the skill:

  1. Which rows? Every condition in the question — still out, this term, longer than a month — narrows the set of rows before anything else is allowed to happen.
  2. Which columns? A question rarely wants a whole record. Naming the columns you actually need is what turns a screen of data into an answer somebody can read aloud.
  3. Rows, or a summary of rows? How many, how much and on average are not questions about rows at all. They collapse many rows into a single value for each group.

The language that writes those decisions down is SQL, the structured query language, and it is broadly the same language whichever database system you meet. Each decision has its own word, and reading them in this order makes a query far less mysterious than it looks:

  • FROM names the table the rows come from, and so decides what is being counted before anything else in the query happens at all.
  • WHERE keeps only the rows that satisfy a condition, and because it runs before any total exists it silently determines every number that follows.
  • SELECT names the columns that come back, and a calculation such as sessions booked minus sessions attended can be one of them, given a name of its own.
  • GROUP BY collapses the surviving rows into one row for each distinct value, which is what lets a count or a sum report per category instead of per record.
  • HAVING filters those grouped rows, and it exists because WHERE has already finished its work by the time any total has been calculated.
  • ORDER BY and LIMIT sort the result and keep only the first few rows, which together answer anything phrased as the busiest, the longest, or the worst three.

Here is one whole query over a table of lesson sign-ups: SELECT Learner, Fee FROM signups WHERE Term = 'Spring' ORDER BY Fee DESC. Read it as four decisions in a row. The rows come from the sign-up table; only spring sign-ups survive; two columns come back, the learner and the fee; and the result arrives dearest first. Nothing in it names a particular learner, which is why the same query still works after another hundred sign-ups arrive.

Before writing one yourself it is worth being deliberate about the order of thinking, because a query that runs is not the same thing as a query that answers the question you were asked.

Sequence

From a business question to a query you can trust

Put the five steps into the order that produces an answer to the question actually asked, then read why each one sits where it does.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

The hardest part of querying is not the words. It is resisting the urge to start typing before the question has been stated precisely enough to be answered. These five steps are the same discipline the earlier modules asked for when turning evidence into a claim.

  1. State the question in ordinary business words, and name the decision the answer feeds. “Which instruments are out right now, and who has them?” is a question; “have a look at the loans” is not. — A query can only be as precise as the sentence behind it. Naming the decision the answer serves is what stops you producing a screen of rows that is technically correct and useless, because nobody can act on it.
  2. Find where the fact is stored: which table has one row for each thing the question is about, and which other table holds the extra detail the question also mentions. — The question mentions instruments and people, and those are two different kinds of thing. The table you count from is the one whose rows are the units being asked about, which here is loans rather than members.
  3. Decide which rows. Every condition in the question — still out, this term, longer than a month — has to be written down as a filter before anything is counted. — The filter runs before any total exists, so whatever it excludes is missing from every number that follows. Most confidently wrong answers were produced by a filter that nobody went back and read.
  4. Decide what comes back: the rows themselves with the columns the question mentions, or one summary value for each group when the question asks how many, how much, or how long on average. — Choosing rows and choosing columns are separate decisions, and summarising is a third. A question about loans per town does not want the loans at all; it wants one line per town, which is a different result rather than a different layout.
  5. Run it, then read the result back against the original question and satisfy yourself that it answers that question rather than a neighbouring one. — A query that runs is not a query that is right. The commonest failure is a clean answer to a slightly different question — every loan rather than every loan still out — and only rereading the question catches it.

Asking one table a question

The table below records lesson sign-ups at that same hypothetical music school. Everything in it is invented for practice, every person named included. Each row is one sign-up, carrying the learner, the instrument, the level, the term, how many sessions were booked, how many were attended, and the fee.

Write a query for each question and run it. Any query that returns the right answer is accepted rather than only the wording that happened to be expected, so there is more than one way through. When a query cannot run, the page says why in plain language, which teaches more than an empty result would.

Database

Question one table

Write a SELECT for each question and run it. Any query that returns the right answer is accepted, so there is more than one correct way through.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

signups — RecordID, Learner, Instrument, Level, Term, Sessions, Attended, Fee (10 rows)

1. List the learner and the instrument for every sign-up at the beginner level.

SELECT Learner, Instrument FROM signups WHERE Level = 'beginner'

SELECT chooses the columns and WHERE chooses the rows. They are two independent decisions, and confusing them is the most common early mistake: asking for fewer columns never removes a row.

2. Show every sign-up with the learner, the instrument, and the number of sessions missed, with the worst attendance first.

SELECT Learner, Instrument, Sessions - Attended AS Missed FROM signups ORDER BY Missed DESC

Missed sessions are nowhere in the table; they are worked out as the query runs. Naming the calculation with AS is what lets ORDER BY refer to it, and it also gives the reader a heading that says what the number means.

3. Which instruments does the school actually teach? List each one once.

SELECT DISTINCT Instrument FROM signups

DISTINCT answers a question about the set of values rather than about the records. It is the smallest example of the difference between listing rows and describing them, which is what grouping does at greater scale.

4. Name the three most expensive sign-ups, showing the learner, the instrument and the fee.

SELECT Learner, Instrument, Fee FROM signups ORDER BY Fee DESC LIMIT 3

Questions phrased as the worst three or the busiest five are a sort followed by a cut, not a filter. Nobody could have written a WHERE for this, because the threshold depends on the data rather than on the question.

Notice what the second question needed. The number of missed sessions is not stored anywhere; it is worked out from two columns at the moment you ask. Storing it as well would create a third value that can disagree with the other two, which is the trouble with the files all over again in miniature. Facts that can be derived are generally derived rather than kept.

Questions no single row can answer

Everything so far returned rows that already existed. Two kinds of question do not work that way, and between them they cover most of what management actually asks for.

  • Summaries ask about groups rather than records — how many loans per instrument, or how long the average loan runs, produce one line for each group and no underlying rows at all.
  • Joins ask about facts that were deliberately kept apart — who the borrower is and what they borrowed are two different kinds of fact living in two tables, and a join matches them on the value they share.
  • Filters can apply before or after the grouping — keeping only the loans still out is a condition on rows, while keeping only the instruments borrowed more than once is a condition on a total that does not exist until the grouping has finished.

The two tables below belong to the same hypothetical school, and again every member and every loan in them is invented. One holds a row for each member, with the town they live in and the date they joined; the other holds a row for each loan, carrying a member identifier rather than a name.

Database

Two tables, and questions about groups

Each question needs either a join, a grouping, or both; run each query and compare the result with what the question actually asked for.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

members — MemberID, Name, Town, JoinedOn (6 rows)

loans — LoanID, MemberID, Instrument, Status, Weeks (10 rows)

1. Which instruments are out at the moment, and who has them? Show the member’s name and the instrument.

SELECT m.Name, l.Instrument FROM loans l JOIN members m ON l.MemberID = m.MemberID WHERE l.Status = 'out'

A join puts related rows from two tables side by side on a matching value. Notice that the name is stored once and borrowed by the query, which is precisely why correcting it in one place corrects every answer.

2. How many times has each instrument been loaned? Show the most borrowed first.

SELECT Instrument, COUNT(*) AS Loans FROM loans GROUP BY Instrument ORDER BY Loans DESC

Grouping turns a list of events into a description of them. The result has one row per instrument and none of the original loans, which is the clearest illustration that a summary is a different answer rather than a tidier one.

3. Which instruments have been borrowed more than once? Show the instrument and the number of loans, busiest first.

SELECT Instrument, COUNT(*) AS Loans FROM loans GROUP BY Instrument HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY Loans DESC

WHERE filters rows and HAVING filters groups. Putting the count condition in WHERE fails because at that stage nothing has been counted yet, and the distinction becomes intuitive once you read a query in execution order rather than in writing order.

4. How many loans has each town produced? Show the busiest town first.

SELECT m.Town, COUNT(*) AS Loans FROM loans l JOIN members m ON l.MemberID = m.MemberID GROUP BY m.Town ORDER BY Loans DESC

This answer exists in neither table. Nobody recorded a town against a loan, yet the question is answerable because the two facts were stored in a way that lets them be brought together on demand.

5. For loans that have already come back, how long did they run on average?

SELECT AVG(Weeks) AS AvgWeeks FROM loans WHERE Status = 'returned'

The filter decides the answer here as much as the function does: including loans that are still out would average an unfinished length against finished ones. An average is only as honest as the set of rows underneath it.

The last questions are the ones worth sitting with. Neither answer exists in any row: the count for each town is assembled at the moment of asking, out of records that were never entered with towns in mind. That is the practical difference between a set of files and a database — files answer the questions they were built for, and a database answers questions nobody had thought of when the records were written.

What renting takes off your hands, and what stays yours

The service models earlier in this module decide who installs and patches the database software. They do not decide who is responsible for the data, and that confusion is what this section exists to prevent.

  1. Infrastructure as a service. You are given processing, storage and networking, and everything above that is yours: the operating system, the database software, its licence, its updates and its backups.
  2. Platform as a service. The provider supplies and updates the platform, database management system included, so the licence and the patching stop being your problem. The chapter names that saving explicitly.
  3. Software as a service. You use a finished application, so you choose settings and you own the records inside it, and nothing underneath is visible to you at all.

What none of the three takes away is the design. Which records exist, how they relate to one another, what has to be unique, what a column is allowed to contain, and which questions the store must be able to answer are decisions about the organization rather than about the software. A rented platform will hold whatever shape you give it, including a poor one, and will hold it very reliably indeed.

Check yourself

Who is responsible for the data

Each question is about where responsibility sits rather than about syntax; read every explanation before moving on.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A hypothetical town archive moves its catalogue onto a rented platform, where the provider supplies and updates the database software. Which statement is accurate?

  • A. The archive no longer has to decide what counts as a catalogue record or which questions the catalogue must be able to answer, because a rented platform arrives with both of those already settled — A platform supplies a general-purpose place to keep records. It has no view about what an archive record ought to contain, and it will accept an incoherent design as readily as a good one.
  • B. The archive keeps paying the database licence but gives up control of how the catalogue is designed — This has the trade-off backwards. The platform model is defined by the licence and the platform maintenance moving to the provider, and design was never something the provider held.
  • C. The archive stops buying and patching the database software, and still decides which records exist, how they relate, what must be unique, and which questions the catalogue has to answer — correct. The licence, the patching and the underlying machines move to the provider; the meaning of the data does not move anywhere, because it was never a technical question in the first place.
  • D. A rented platform cannot host a catalogue, because a catalogue needs database software the archive installs on its own machines — Hosting a catalogue is ordinary platform work. Nothing about a catalogue requires locally installed software, which is why so many organizations run this kind of store on rented platforms.

2. A hypothetical youth theatre runs its booking system on the infrastructure service model. Who is responsible for the database software it depends on?

  • A. The theatre, because that model supplies processing, storage and networking, and everything from the operating system upward is the customer’s to install, licence and patch — correct. The chapter describes that model as providing only the basic capabilities of processing, storage and networking, which is also why it says the customer keeps the most control and keeps responsibility for managing software licences.
  • B. The provider, because supplying storage necessarily includes supplying the software that organizes what is stored — Storage in this sense means space and the machines that hold it. Organizing what goes into that space is exactly the work the customer takes on in exchange for the extra control.
  • C. Neither, because on that model the database runs as a shared service used by every customer on the same machines — That describes a shared service somebody else operates, which is a different model. Here the customer receives raw capacity and decides what runs on it.
  • D. The theatre for the software and the provider for the data held inside it, which is the division of responsibility that this service model was designed around and the reason it costs less than the alternative — The split is the other way round in one half and wrong in the other: the customer runs the software, and the data inside it is the customer’s responsibility on every one of the three models.

3. A hypothetical dental practice proposes recording far more detail about every appointment so that it can analyse patterns later. Which cost picture matches what the chapter says?

  • A. A single one-off cost, since the records are captured by staff who are already there and stored on machines the practice already owns — The capture is close to free and the keeping is not. Data recorded once has to be stored, backed up, moved and eventually archived for as long as the practice keeps it, which is a commitment rather than a purchase.
  • B. A rise in storage only, because processing and software costs are fixed regardless of how much data is kept — Storage is the visible cost and rarely the only one. Analysing a much larger set of records needs hardware that can work through it, which is why the chapter names the two together.
  • C. A rise in bandwidth only, because the extra detail has to travel between the practice and wherever it is stored — Bandwidth does grow with richer content, and the chapter makes that point about video. It is one strand of the story rather than the whole of it, and the practice would still be paying to keep and process everything it sent.
  • D. More storage space, more capable hardware to process the data, and database software to manage and analyse it — three running costs from one decision — correct. The chapter states it plainly: capturing more data requires ever more storage space, ever more powerful computing hardware, and database management systems to manage and analyse it. Deciding to record something is deciding to pay for it repeatedly.

The hand-off to SQLite

Everything above is about reading. Building is the other half, and it is where the course goes next. SQLite is a database system that keeps an entire database in a single ordinary file and runs inside the program using it, with no separate server to install or keep running. That makes it an unusually honest place to learn, because nothing between you and the data is hidden behind an administrator.

The queries on this page are the same language you will write there. What changes is that you will also decide what the tables are: which things deserve a table of their own, which column identifies a row, and which questions the design has to answer on the day somebody finally asks. Creating a database application in SQLite is the course’s own separate work, and this supplement is the bridge to it rather than a substitute for it.

The container can be rented; the meaning cannot. Somebody in the organization still has to know what a record is, which is why a section about tables belongs in a module about machines.

What to carry out of this sectionOne stored set of records, one home for each fact, and questions asked of the store rather than answers copied out of it. If you can say which rows a claim rests on and which columns it reads, you can defend it. If the claim arrived as a file somebody mailed you, all you can do is repeat it.

Application supplement · 3–6

The internet as a business tool

Everything in this section has already appeared somewhere in this module: the internet, the web, intranets and extranets, the copies of pages held near users, the interfaces that let one application ask another a question. What the chapter never does is set those pieces side by side and ask the plain business question — what does a company actually use all of this for? The answer is three things, and telling them apart comes down to one decision, taken by a person rather than by a machine.

How this supplement relates to the chapter. Chapter 3 teaches each of these parts where it belongs, as infrastructure. This supplement reassembles them around the audience being served, because that is the shape the course’s own objective takes: using internet technology for electronic commerce, for communicating with employees, and for working with business partners. It is a labeled application supplement rather than a textbook learning objective, it adds no claim the chapter does not already make, and every organization used for practice in it is hypothetical and invented.

Three jobs, one set of parts

Begin with the fact that makes this genuinely confusing rather than merely new. A browser asking a server for a page behaves in exactly the same way whether the person reading it is a shopper, a member of staff, or a supplier’s dispatcher. Same request, same protocol, same page arriving. The technology has no opinion about who is at the other end of it.

What differs is who is authorized, and that is a decision somebody in the organization has to take before any system can enforce it. The chapter’s comparison of the internet, an intranet and an extranet, which you met earlier in this module, separates the three by focus, content, users and access rather than by what they are built from. Read that table again and it turns out to be a table of audiences.

Those audiences are the three jobs, and they are worth naming plainly before anything is built for them.

  • Selling to customers — general, public content that anyone with an internet connection may read, which is the arrangement the chapter calls the internet, and which almost every organization now depends on to take money at all.
  • Communicating with employees — specific, corporate and proprietary content restricted to authorized employees, which is the arrangement the chapter calls an intranet, and which quietly replaced an enormous amount of paper.
  • Working with business partners — communications between two or more firms doing business together, restricted to authorized partners, which is the arrangement the chapter calls an extranet and carries over the public internet.

Three audiences, one technology, one decision. Everything that follows is a consequence of that, including the expensive mistakes at the end of the section.

Selling to customers: almost any business is an e-business

The chapter states it without qualification: today, almost any business can be considered an e-business. That sentence is stronger than it first looks, because it does not say almost any business sells online. It says the business now runs on its data being reachable — and once that is true, the wire and the server are part of the trading position whether or not one item is ever bought on the site.

A hypothetical example makes the range obvious. A veterinary practice that publishes nothing but its address, its opening hours and a booking form has still put its bookings on the internet. When that page fails to load on a Monday morning, appointments are not made and the money is not taken. Data are the lifeblood of almost all organizations, so reliably accessing them is a key concern, which is the chapter’s reason for caring about availability at all.

Four demands follow from that, and every one of them was taught earlier in this module as a piece of infrastructure rather than as a commercial requirement. Assembled, they are what selling over the internet actually asks of a company.

  • Answering while the customer is still there — operational data for a site where response time is of the essence belongs on fast disk-based storage, and on flash-based storage where access speed is of crucial importance, because a page that arrives late has already lost the sale.
  • Surviving the busiest fortnight of the year — firms engaged in or supporting business-to-consumer electronic commerce meet a large spike in demand before the December holidays, and the capacity that felt generous in March is what decides how that fortnight goes.
  • Closing the distance — the greater the geographical distance between a user and the server holding the content, the longer that content takes to arrive, which is the delay a network of servers holding copies in several locations exists to remove.
  • Being available at all — organizations that depend on trading electronically strive for the highest availability of their hardware, storage and networking components, and the five-nines target the chapter describes leaves just over five minutes of downtime in a year.

Notice what kind of decisions those are. Not one of them is a marketing decision, and not one of them can be taken after the campaign has been booked. For a business selling over the internet the shopfront is the infrastructure, which is the whole of the chapter’s argument for why a manager should care about plumbing.

Check yourself

Selling over the internet, and what it demands underneath

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for the options you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A hypothetical veterinary practice takes no payments on its website and sells nothing there. Its owner says the practice is therefore not an e-business and does not need to think about availability. Which reading matches the chapter?

  • A. Almost any business can be considered an e-business, so the real question is what happens to the practice on a morning when its data are not reachable — correct. The chapter says that today almost any business can be considered an e-business, and that because data are the lifeblood of almost all organizations, reliably accessing those data is a key concern rather than an optional refinement.
  • B. The owner is right, because being an e-business means selling goods or services over the internet and the practice does neither — This reads e-business as a synonym for online retailing, which is narrower than the chapter’s claim. The practice’s bookings, records and opening information already depend on the same infrastructure a retailer’s orders depend on.
  • C. The practice becomes an e-business only once it accepts card payment on the site, since a completed transaction is what makes trading electronic — Payment is one thing a site can do, not the thing that makes a business dependent on the internet. A booking form that stops working costs the practice appointments long before any card is presented.
  • D. The distinction does not matter, because availability targets apply to organizations large enough to run a data center of their own — Availability is about whether the organization can reach and be reached, and the chapter attaches it to being data-intensive rather than to owning a facility. A small practice renting everything still loses the morning when the pages do not load.

2. A hypothetical ticket seller’s pages take several seconds to appear while a customer sits waiting, and the delay is in reading the records the page is built from. Which of the chapter’s storage decisions is at stake?

  • A. Archival storage, since these records are being kept for the long term and it is the archive the customer is really waiting on while the assistant apologizes for the delay — Archival data are long-term copies held for compliance and reporting, typically on tape, where data sit sequentially so access is slow and not quickly searchable. That is the wrong medium for anything a person is waiting on.
  • B. Backup storage, since the recovery copy is what would be read if the main records were slow to answer — Backup data are short-term copies for recovering from a disaster, and the chapter’s reason for keeping them on hard drives is quick recovery. They are not the copy a page is built from during normal trading.
  • C. Operational data belongs on fast disk-based storage where response time is of the essence, and on flash-based storage where access speed is of crucial importance — correct. The chapter puts operational data on disk-based media precisely because hard drives offer high access speeds where response time matters, and names an e-commerce site as its example, with flash used where speed is crucial.
  • D. None of these, because the delay a customer experiences is decided by bandwidth rather than by where the records are kept — Bandwidth is the capacity of the pathway, and widening it does not help when the time is being spent reading a record before anything is sent. The two delays have different causes and different remedies.

3. A hypothetical gift retailer’s site is slow for two separate reasons: everybody arrives at once in the fortnight before the holidays, and customers on another continent wait noticeably longer than customers at home. Which pairing matches the chapter’s account?

  • A. Both are capacity problems at heart, so one larger server at the retailer’s own site answers the seasonal slowness and the overseas delay together, and no second arrangement is needed — A larger server does nothing about distance. The overseas customer is waiting on transmission across a long path, and that wait is unchanged by how quickly the far end could have replied.
  • B. Both are distance problems, since a network carrying more traffic behaves like a longer one — Congestion and distance both add delay, but the chapter treats them separately: one is demand exceeding capacity in a fortnight, the other is the geographical gap between a user and the server holding the content.
  • C. The seasonal slowness is a bandwidth shortage and the overseas delay is a storage shortage — Neither label fits. The December problem is a fluctuation in demand rather than a fixed shortage, and the overseas delay is caused by the length of the path, not by where the records are stored.
  • D. The seasonal slowness is a demand fluctuation answered by capacity that can grow and shrink; the overseas delay is distance, answered by copies of the content held near those users — correct. The chapter treats the pre-holiday spike as a demand fluctuation, and treats distance as its own cause of latency answered by a network of servers in various geographical locations holding copies, the nearest one delivering the content.

Communicating with employees: the inside of the building, from anywhere

The second audience is the organization’s own staff, and the arrangement built for them is the intranet you met earlier: the same web technologies, secured with authentication techniques, firewalls, or both, so that proprietary material is visible only to authorized users. What is worth adding here is not the definition but the accounting — what each internal use replaced, and why the replacement costs less.

The chapter names five internal uses. Read them as a column of things that somebody used to do by hand.

Internal useWhat it replacesWhat changes as a result
Disseminating corporate informationA notice sent round the building and kept in whichever copy each person happened to saveOne current copy in one place, so arguments about what the policy says stop happening
Employee trainingScheduling everybody into a room on a day that suits almost nobodyStaff work through the material from any desk, on their own schedule
Project managementStatus reported upward, rewritten, and then redistributed downwardEvery member of the project sees the same plan and the same state at the same moment
CollaborationDocuments mailed back and forth between departments and buildingsPeople in different places work on one thing rather than on parallel copies of it
Employee self-serviceA form completed by a member of staff and then keyed in by somebody in an officeThe work moves to the person who already knows the answer, and one keystroke disappears

Only the last row saves money you could point at in a budget, and it is the row to hold on to, because the same move reappears in the next audience. Nothing there was automated. A step was deleted, because the person who held the information was finally allowed to record it directly.

Then there is the question of where the employee is standing. An intranet reachable only from a desk inside the building serves a workforce that is increasingly not inside the building, so most companies let employees use a virtual private network to connect securely to the intranet while travelling or working from home.

The audience has not changed there; only the road has. It is the same promise the cloud characteristic called broad network access makes when it says a service is available from almost anywhere and from almost any web-enabled device — the same internal material, on whatever device the person happens to have with them.

Working with partners: the second keystroke

The third audience is the other companies the organization depends on: the supplier who has to know what to ship, the haulier who has to know what to collect, the laboratory running the samples. They are not employees, so the intranet is shut to them. They are not the public, so the public site tells them nothing they need. The chapter’s answer is the extranet — a private part of the internet reachable by authorized business partners after logging on, and usually secured with a tunnel.

The interesting part is not the arrangement itself but the failure it removes. Follow one hypothetical order through two companies that share nothing, and watch where the cost appears.

  1. The buyer records the order. A purchasing clerk enters the quantities into the buyer’s own system, which becomes one authoritative record, and emails a copy of it across to the supplier.
  2. The supplier records it again. Somebody at the supplier reads that email and types the same quantities into a different system, creating a second record that merely resembles the first one.
  3. The buyer changes something. A quantity is revised and a second email goes out, so the supplier’s record is now a version behind, and nothing in either system says which of the two numbers counts.
  4. The goods arrive. The disagreement surfaces in the receiving bay, the most expensive place in either company to find it, and settling it costs a phone call, a credit note, and sometimes a second lorry.

Nobody in that story was careless. The error was manufactured by step two, and step two exists only because two firms keep separate copies of one fact. The chapter’s name for removing it is a single point of data entry, from which data can be updated on disparate corporate computing platforms without having to be reentered — and the benefit that sounds clerical is the one that turns up in the accounts.

Three more of the chapter’s partner benefits are worth reading as business outcomes rather than as features of a product.

  • Automating business transactions — moving orders, confirmations and invoices through a system rather than through people reduces processing costs and cycle times, which is to say both the money spent and the time spent waiting.
  • Real-time data for management — because transactions arrive as they happen, management can obtain real-time data with which to track and analyze business activities, instead of waiting for a summary written after the month it describes.
  • Central management of documents — one managed copy reduces the number of versions in circulation and the amount of out-of-date information stored in various places, which matters most when the other reader works for a different firm.

There is a version of this same relationship with the people taken out of it altogether. An interface between applications lets one organization’s system use a service another organization provides, without knowing how that service is produced, by passing agreed values and receiving an answer back. A shared web area lets two firms read one record; an interface lets their two systems do it unattended. The principle is identical — an agreed shape, one authoritative answer — with the browser and the clerk removed.

The situations below are all hypothetical and invented. Sort each one by the audience it is really serving, because that is the decision that settles everything else about it.

Sort

Which audience is this really serving?

Place each situation with the use it serves. Every organization below is a hypothetical practice situation, and each one states the conditions you need in order to decide.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Selling to customers — general, public content that anyone with an internet connection may read, with access public and not restricted

  • A hypothetical bakery publishes its product range, its opening hours and an order form that anybody who finds the site can use — General, public content readable by anyone with an internet connection, with access public and not restricted — the chapter’s own description of the internet, and the reason nothing goes here that the bakery would not tell a stranger.
  • A hypothetical bus operator publishes its timetable for any passenger to check, and the pages are copied to servers in several regions so they load quickly wherever the passenger is — Public content plus a content delivery network, which the chapter describes as the way to reduce the delay caused by geographical distance. The copies change how fast the public is served, not who is served.
  • A hypothetical museum lets a visitor reserve a timed entry from home at eleven at night, weeks before arriving — The museum sells nothing on the page beyond a place in a queue, and it is still trading electronically: almost any business can be considered an e-business, and the booking is taken from a member of the public with no account and no prior relationship.

Communicating with employees — specific, corporate and proprietary content, restricted to authorized employees or members, with access private and restricted

  • Staff at a hypothetical building society open a page from their own desks and enrol in this year’s health cover without sending a form to anybody — Employee self-service through a portal is one of the five internal uses the chapter names for an intranet, and the content is proprietary and restricted to authorized employees.
  • Shift supervisors at a hypothetical parcel depot read the week’s safety notices and finish a required training module from any depot in the country — Two of the chapter’s named intranet uses at once, disseminating corporate information and employee training, both restricted to the organization’s own staff wherever in the country they are working.
  • Site surveyors at a hypothetical engineering firm open the internal drawing archive from a hotel, through a secured tunnel, rather than from the office — A virtual private network changes where the employee is standing, not who the audience is. The chapter treats the tunnel as the way an intranet reaches a mobile workforce, and the content remains internal.

Working with partners — communications between two or more firms doing business together, restricted to authorized business partners

  • A hypothetical dairy cooperative gives each of its two haulage contractors a login to see tomorrow’s collection schedule and confirm the volumes lifted today — Two firms using the internet to do business together, reachable only by authorized business partners after logging on. The confirmation is also the single point of data entry that spares both sides from keying the same volume twice.
  • A hypothetical seed laboratory posts every test result it produces into an area that its two client growers can read the moment the result exists — Content whose focus is communication between business partners, private and restricted to authorized partners, and an example of the real-time visibility the chapter lists among the benefits of working this way.
  • A hypothetical grain merchant’s system asks a haulier’s system directly for a delivery slot and receives an answer, with nobody at either firm involved — This is the machine-to-machine version of the same partner relationship: a service consumer uses a provider’s service without knowing how it is produced, by passing agreed values. The browser and the clerk are gone; the audience is not.

Getting the audience wrong

In practice the wrong answer here is almost never a technology. It is publishing to the wrong audience, and there are three familiar ways of doing that, each of which looks like a shortcut on the day it is taken.

  • Internal material on the public site — usually done to avoid the trouble of managing accounts, and it works right up until somebody notices that proprietary content has become general content and cannot be called back.
  • Obscurity mistaken for restriction — an unlinked page that no search engine has indexed is still reachable by anyone holding the address, which is why the chapter treats authentication and firewalls, rather than not being linked to, as what makes content private.
  • Partners handed employee access — the quickest way to let an outside firm see one schedule is to give it a staff login, and doing so grants that firm everything else an employee can reach along with it.

Each of those is a decision about people wearing a technical costume. That is precisely why the person who should be answering it is somebody who understands the business rather than somebody who understands the servers.

Work the four decisions below in order, and read every outcome before moving on — including the outcomes of the choices you did not make.

Decide

Four requests in one week

Work the four decisions in order, and after each one compare every outcome before moving on.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

A hypothetical practice situation. You have taken over systems and communications at an invented regional food cooperative that sells produce boxes to the public, employs about forty people across three sites, and works with two haulage contractors. Four requests land in your first week. Each one looks like a technology question and is really a question about which audience is being served.

Decision 1. The membership secretary wants the annual report, the monthly member notices and the compulsory food-handling training module put on the public website, so that members can always find them and nobody has to manage accounts.

  • Put them behind authentication as an intranet for authorized members, and leave the public site to the catalogue. — the stronger call. Right. Same web technologies, different audience, different access rule: internal communications, specific and proprietary content, authorized users, private and restricted. Notice that you decided this by naming the reader, not by comparing products — which is what makes it a management decision rather than a technical one.
  • Publish them on the public site as asked, since nobody outside the cooperative would go looking for member notices. — The chapter treats authentication and firewalls, not the unlikelihood of being found, as what makes content private. Member notices and a training module are proprietary content, and once they are public they are readable by any competitor, any journalist and any search engine, permanently and without your knowing.
  • Publish them on the public site but leave them unlinked from the menu, so only members who were sent the address can reach them. — An unlinked page is exactly the third kind of content the chapter puts in the deep web: invisible to a search engine and reachable by anyone holding the address. It is one forwarded email away from being fully public, and nothing in the arrangement will tell you when that happens.
  • Issue every member an account on the extranet the cooperative already runs with its two haulage contractors. — It would work on the day, and it dissolves the boundary you will later be asked to audit. The chapter defines an extranet’s users as authorized business partners; putting several hundred members inside it gives them the partner content too, and leaves you unable to say who may see the collection schedules.

Decision 2. The public produce-box shop runs at a steady level for most of the year. In the fortnight before the December holidays orders run several times higher, and last year the site was slow enough that customers abandoned their baskets. The equipment currently sits in a room at the main site.

  • Move the public shop onto rented capacity that grows and shrinks with demand, and serve the pages and images from copies held near customers. — the stronger call. Right, and note that it is two answers to two different problems. Capacity that can grow and shrink answers the seasonal fluctuation the chapter describes for December electronic commerce; copies held in several geographical locations answer the delay caused by distance. Neither one fixes the other.
  • Buy a second server sized for the December fortnight and keep it in the room with the first. — This is the demand-fluctuation problem the chapter describes, met in the most expensive way available. Capacity bought in whole units leaves idle resources for most of the year, and what you have actually purchased, permanently, is a fortnight. It may be the only option if you must own the equipment, but it should be chosen knowingly.
  • Ask customers to place their holiday orders earlier in the season so the load is spread out. — This asks the customer to solve the cooperative’s capacity problem, and most of them will simply buy elsewhere in the fortnight when they were going to buy anyway. For a business selling over the internet the site is the shop, and telling shoppers to come at a quieter time is closing the door at the busiest hour.
  • Reduce the size of the product photographs so that each page is smaller. — It genuinely helps, and it is not enough. Smaller pages reduce the bytes each visitor pulls but not the number of visitors arriving at once, so the peak still exceeds what the room can serve. It is also a poor trade for a business whose product is food that people buy by looking at it.

Decision 3. The two haulage contractors currently receive collection schedules by email and retype them into their own systems. Twice this year a lorry arrived for a volume that had been revised after the email went out, and both times the cooperative and the contractor each produced a document proving they were right.

  • Give both contractors access to the schedule where it is maintained, and let them confirm the lifted volume in the same place. — the stronger call. Right. This is the chapter’s single point of data entry, from which data can be updated on disparate corporate computing platforms without being reentered. One record exists, so there is nothing left for the two firms to disagree about, and management gets real-time data on what was actually lifted rather than a reconciliation after the fact.
  • Send the schedule twice, once as an email and once as an attached spreadsheet, so each contractor can check one against the other. — Two copies do not settle a disagreement; they create a third version and a new question about which one is authoritative. The chapter’s benefit is the removal of the reentry, not better documentation of it, and every extra copy is another thing that can be a version behind.
  • Publish the collection schedule on the public site so the contractors can always see the current version. — It does make the schedule current, and it also tells every competitor what this cooperative moves, from where, and on which days. The content’s focus is communication between business partners, and the chapter makes that category private and restricted for exactly this reason.
  • Require both contractors to telephone the depot each morning to confirm the day’s volumes before loading. — A call is simply a third place for the number to be transcribed, and it adds a person to a process that is failing because of people copying figures. It also produces nothing management can track or analyze, since the confirmation exists only in somebody’s memory of the conversation.

Decision 4. Six delivery drivers and two field buyers are almost never at a desk. They need the week’s notices, the compulsory training module, and a way to file expense claims from wherever they happen to be.

  • Let them reach the same internal pages the office staff use, over a secured tunnel from whatever device they carry. — the stronger call. Right. Increases in employee mobility are the chapter’s own reason for virtual private networks: staff connect securely to the intranet while travelling or working away from the office. The audience did not change, so the arrangement should not either — only the road into it is different.
  • Email the notices out weekly and have the drivers post paper expense forms back to the office. — This is precisely the arrangement the intranet replaced. Notices sit in eight separate mailboxes with no way to tell who is reading a superseded one, and every posted form is a keystroke for somebody in an office — the work that employee self-service was named for removing.
  • Publish the notices and the training module on the public site and accept expense claims by email, since these people are outside the building anyway. — Being outside the building is a location, not an audience. The chapter separates these arrangements by who is authorized, and a driver in a lay-by is still an employee, so putting internal material in front of the general public to reach eight of them is a large exposure for a small convenience.
  • Give each of them a laptop with a copy of the internal pages stored on it, so no connection is needed at all. — A copy taken on Monday is wrong by Tuesday. The chapter’s observation that very little information in business is static is the whole reason internal communication moved onto web technologies in the first place, and eight stored copies recreate exactly the problem one current copy was there to solve.

Reading it back to the objective

The course objective this supplement serves has three clauses, and each one now has an arrangement, a set of demands on the infrastructure, and a question that decides which of the three you are in. That is the whole of it, and it fits in one table.

The useThe arrangementWhat the infrastructure has to deliverThe question that settles it
Electronic commerceThe public internetFast storage, capacity that survives the peak, copies held near the customer, and availabilityWould we be content for a stranger to read this?
Communicating with employeesAn intranet, reached from outside through a secured tunnelAuthentication, one current copy of everything, and reach to wherever the staff actually areIs this reader on our payroll or our membership roll?
Working with partnersAn extranet, or an interface between the two firms’ systemsOne authoritative record both firms work from, and transactions that arrive as they happenIs this a firm we have agreed to do business with, and what exactly may it see?

One set of web technologies, three audiences, separated by who is authorized — and the separation is drawn by a manager naming the reader, not by a product being purchased.

One last pass over the three uses before the module closes.

Check yourself

Three uses, one technology

Four options, one best answer; the explanations are where the distinctions live, so read all four.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. According to the chapter, what actually separates the internet, an intranet and an extranet from one another?

  • A. The software and networking technologies each is built from, since the three arrangements use different products — The chapter says the opposite: an intranet uses the same software, hardware and networking technologies as a publicly accessible website. Nothing in the comparison table mentions a product at all.
  • B. Whether the traffic crosses the public internet, since intranet traffic stays inside the organization and extranet traffic does not — This is nearly true and still unreliable. The simplest form of an intranet does stay within organizational boundaries, but most companies let employees reach the intranet over a tunnel across the public internet, so the route cannot be the divider.
  • C. Who is authorized to see the content, since the three carry different content for different audiences under different access rules — correct. The chapter’s table separates the three by focus, type of content, users and access: public content for anyone with a connection, corporate and proprietary content for authorized employees, and partner communications for authorized business partners.
  • D. Which department owns the pages, since internal pages belong with human resources and partner pages belong with purchasing — Ownership inside the organization is a question of who maintains the pages, not of who may read them. Two arrangements owned by the same department can still face entirely different audiences.

2. A hypothetical cannery gives its two ingredient suppliers a shared area in which to confirm each shipment as it leaves. Its operations manager notices she no longer waits for a monthly summary to know what is in transit. Which of the chapter’s stated benefits is she describing?

  • A. Central management of documents, which reduces the number of versions in circulation and the amount of out-of-date information stored around the organization — That benefit is about which copy of a document is the current one. It is real and it is not what changed here: the manager’s complaint was about when she learned something, not about which version she was reading.
  • B. Management can obtain real-time data with which to track and analyze business activities — correct. The chapter lists exactly this among the benefits of working with partners this way, and it follows from the transactions arriving as they happen rather than being gathered up and reported afterwards.
  • C. Automating business transactions, which reduces processing costs and cycle times — Automation lowers what each transaction costs and how long it takes to complete. That is a benefit of the same arrangement, but the manager described visibility of activity rather than cheaper or faster processing.
  • D. The internet can be used as a relatively secure medium over which to do business with another firm — Security is the chapter’s judgment that the public internet can carry this traffic acceptably, which is a precondition for the arrangement existing at all rather than the improvement the manager noticed.

3. A hypothetical wholesaler’s system asks a courier’s system for a delivery slot and receives one back, with nobody at either firm involved. How is this best described, and how does it relate to the shared partner area the two firms already use?

  • A. It is a content delivery arrangement, since the courier is supplying content to the wholesaler across a distance — A content delivery network holds copies of a site closer to its users to reduce the delay caused by distance. Nothing here is about distance, and the courier is answering a question rather than serving a stored page.
  • B. It is a form of intranet, because the two systems are communicating privately rather than publicly — An intranet serves an organization’s own authorized employees. These are two separate firms, which is what makes the relationship a partner arrangement no matter how private the exchange is.
  • C. It replaces the shared partner area entirely, since once two machines exchange the figures directly there is nothing left for a person to log in and read, and the web area can be switched off — The two do different jobs. A shared area lets people at both firms read and confirm records; an interface lets their systems exchange a specific answer unattended, and most partnerships end up using both.
  • D. It is an interface between applications: one program uses another’s service by passing agreed values, without knowing how the result is produced — correct. The chapter defines an interface between applications as letting a service consumer use a service provider’s service without having to know how the underlying service is created, by passing pre-specified values and receiving the requested service back.

Reference

Chapter vocabulary

Every term the chapter defines, in one place, written so it makes sense on its own with an example beside it. Search by word, or filter by the objective the term belongs to. This chapter has more vocabulary than the two before it, and a good deal of the difficulty is pairs of terms that sound almost the same and mean genuinely different things — the deep web and the dark web, an intranet and an extranet, grid computing and cloud computing, a client and a server. Use this while you read rather than after.

3.3AI infrastructure
The hardware and software systems used to support artificial intelligence work. It has special requirements: specialized processors rather than ordinary ones, storage that is both larger and faster than usual, and particular machine learning libraries and frameworks for the people building the models.For example: A company that wants to train its own model discovers it cannot simply run it on the servers it already owns, and has to budget for a different class of machine entirely.
3.2application programming interface (API)
An arrangement that lets one piece of software use a service provided by another without knowing how that service works inside. The consumer passes agreed-on values across and gets a result back, which is why software can be assembled out of parts built by different companies.For example: A ride-hailing app sends a pickup point and a destination to a mapping service and receives the best route, without its developers ever having written a map.
3.2archival data
Long-term copies of organizational data, kept mainly for compliance and reporting rather than for daily use. Because it is rarely read, it can live on slow, cheap, removable media, and it needs a life span measured in years rather than days.For example: Internal email from several years ago that nobody expects to open, but that the organization must be able to produce if it is ever asked to.
3.2assembly language
A very low-level programming language that lets a computer operate quickly and efficiently, and the language operating systems are often written in. Part of an operating system’s job is to insulate everyone else from it.For example: Dragging a file from a flash drive to a hard drive is one gesture for you and a long sequence of low-level instructions underneath, which you never have to see.
3.2backup data
Short-term copies of organizational data, made so the organization can recover from a failure or disaster. Backups are frequently overwritten by newer ones, so their value is in being recent and quick to restore rather than in lasting.For example: Last night’s copy of the order system, held on fast storage so that if this morning’s server fails the business is running again in minutes rather than days.
3.2bandwidth
The transmission capacity of a computer or communications channel, measured in bits per second or multiples of it. It is how much data can reliably be carried in one second, and it is what decides whether a file takes eight seconds or a day and a half to arrive.For example: The same video downloads in seconds over a fiber connection and takes hours over an old telephone modem, because only the capacity of the path changed.
3.2bit
The smallest unit of data used by computers. Human communication is made of words; computer communication is made of bits, and everything sent over a network — a document, a song, a film — is bits, differing only in how many of them there are.For example: A page of text runs to roughly fourteen thousand bytes while a print-quality photograph can be more than two hundred million, which is why one arrives instantly and the other does not.
3.4broad network access
One of the five characteristics of cloud computing: because the services are reached over the internet, they are available from almost anywhere and from almost any web-enabled device. It is what lets a manager act on something without going back to an office.For example: Approving an urgent order from a phone in an airport, using the same system that sits on the desktop back at work.
3.2campus area network
A wide area network that spans several buildings belonging to one organization. It is a middle case between a network inside a single building and one that crosses a city or the world.For example: A hospital group whose clinic, laboratory and administration buildings sit on one site and share one network across all three.
3.4capital expenditure and operational expenditure
Two ways of paying for the same computing. A capital expenditure is money spent up front to own equipment; an operational expenditure is money spent continuously to use a service. Cloud computing converts one into the other, which changes the budget it comes out of and who has to approve it.For example: Buying servers is a large purchase in one year; renting the same capacity is a monthly bill that rises and falls with how much the business actually used.
3.2cascading style sheets (CSS)
The standard used to specify the formatting and layout of the elements on a web page. It separates how a page looks from what the page says, so the wording and the appearance can be changed independently.For example: Changing one style rule makes every heading on a thousand-page site larger, without anyone editing a thousand pages.
3.2central processing unit (CPU)
The general-purpose processor that performs a computer’s calculations. It is built to handle instructions one after another very quickly, which suits ordinary software where each step depends on the result of the last one.For example: Recalculating a spreadsheet, where each formula may need the answer from the formula above it before it can run.
3.2client
Any computer or software application on a network that uses the services a server provides. Clients only request; they do not serve. A client usually has one user, whereas many users share the server it talks to.For example: The mail program on a laptop asks a mail server for new messages; it never answers requests from anyone else.
3.2client-server network
A network in which servers and clients have defined roles, some machines providing services and others only requesting them. It is the normal business arrangement, and nearly everyone at work is using one whether they know it or not.For example: Every desk in an office opening files kept on a shared server rather than on each other’s machines.
3.4cloud computing
A model for enabling convenient, on-demand access over a network to a shared pool of configurable computing resources — networks, servers, storage, applications and services — that can be provisioned and released quickly with minimal management effort or interaction with the provider. In plainer words: computing rented by the hour from somebody else’s building.For example: A company that needs two hundred servers for a week gets them the same afternoon with a payment card and a web page, and stops paying when it stops using them.
3.2collocation facility
A data center managed by a third party that rents space to several organizational customers. The tenant still owns and manages its own servers; what it stops paying for is the building, the power, the cooling and the physical security.For example: A regional firm that puts its own machines in a rented, professionally run room instead of building a server room and a generator of its own.
3.2computer networking
The sharing of data or services between machines. It needs three things and no fewer: a sender and a receiver with something to share, a pathway between them, and rules both sides follow.For example: Two people can only have a conversation if there is something to say, a room to say it in, and a language they both speak; a network is the same three requirements in equipment.
3.3consumerization of IT
The trend in which the devices people choose for themselves arrive at work and have to be integrated into the organization’s infrastructure. It shifts part of the equipment decision away from the technology department and toward the individual.For example: Employees expecting to read work email on their own phones, which the organization must then decide how to secure and support.
3.4content delivery network
A network of servers in different geographical locations that store copies of the same content, so a request is answered by the copy nearest the user. It reduces the delay caused by distance, saves bandwidth, and is invisible to the person browsing.For example: A video that plays instantly for viewers on three continents because each of them is actually being served from a machine a few hundred miles away.
3.2cyber-physical system
A system that integrates computing with physical processes, coordinating software, sensors and mechanical components closely enough to monitor and control something in the real world with a high degree of autonomy. The consequences of a fault are physical, which is what makes securing them different.For example: A factory where sensors, controllers and machines run most of the production line between them and reorganize the work without a person intervening.
3.2dark web
Those areas of the web used for various criminal purposes, typically reachable only with specialized browsers that anonymize the user and hide their traces. It is deliberately hidden, and it is not the same thing as the deep web.For example: A marketplace trading stolen payment card numbers, which no ordinary browser or search engine will take you to.
3.2database
An organized collection of related data held so that it can be stored and retrieved reliably. The chapter treats databases as the thing hardware exists to run and storage exists to hold, which is why a storage decision is really a decision about how well questions can be answered later.For example: A shop’s record of every product, every supplier and every sale, kept once so that a price change is made in one place rather than in four spreadsheets.
3.3database management system
The software that stores data, keeps it consistent, and answers questions about it. The chapter counts it as a third cost of capturing more data, alongside the storage space and the processing power, because somebody has to license, configure and run it.For example: Two clerks record a sale at the same moment and the totals still agree afterwards, which is the software doing work nobody sees.
3.2data center
Dedicated space set aside for an organization’s infrastructure, ranging from a single server room to a building the size of a warehouse. Keeping the equipment in one place makes it easier to manage, repair, upgrade, power, cool and secure.For example: A parcel carrier’s facilities that can run for days on their own generated power, with cooling capacity comparable to that of a whole neighbourhood of houses.
3.2digital density
The rising proportion of an organization’s activity that exists as data and is carried out through connected devices. The chapter names it as the reason a well-functioning infrastructure has become essential rather than merely useful.For example: A delivery that once left only a signed paper docket now leaves a scan at every handover, a location trace and a photograph, so the same journey produces a hundred times the record it used to.
3.2deep web
Those parts of the web that conventional search engines cannot index: pages behind a login, pages generated from a database when somebody asks for them, and pages nothing links to. Most of the web is like this, and none of it is necessarily sinister.For example: Your own course pages, your bank statements and an online store’s product listings are all invisible to a search engine, for three different reasons.
3.2desktop virtualization
Providing workers with a desktop environment that actually runs on a server rather than on the machine in front of them. It reduces the cost of licensing and maintaining software and helps with strict privacy and data protection duties, because the data never leaves the data center.For example: A hospital where every screen shows the same working environment, and nothing is stored on the terminal itself if it is stolen.
3.2device driver
Software that allows a computer to communicate with a particular piece of hardware. It is the translation layer between one general operating system and the specific behaviour of one make and model of device.For example: Plugging in an unfamiliar printer and having the computer fetch the small piece of software that teaches it how to talk to that printer.
3.2domain name
The part of a web address that helps a person recognize the company or individual it belongs to. Names exist because the numeric addresses machines actually use are hard to remember and can change.For example: Seeing a familiar name in the address bar tells you whose server you have reached, which a string of numbers would not.
3.2e-business
A business whose ordinary operations depend on internet technology rather than merely using it at the edges. The chapter’s position is that almost any business today can be considered one, which is what makes infrastructure everyone’s problem rather than the technology department’s.For example: A family bakery that takes orders on a website, buys flour through a supplier portal and rosters staff in a shared calendar is running on the internet even though nobody there would call it a technology company.
3.4edge computing
What content delivery networks grew into: moving not only stored data but also the processing away from one central location out to the edges of the network, close to where the data is produced. The point is to cut the delay, and secondarily to cut traffic and cost.For example: A monitoring device that decides for itself that a reading is dangerous, instead of sending every reading across the country and waiting for an answer.
3.2embedded system
A computer designed to perform one specific set of tasks well, built into something that is not thought of as a computer. It has no general-purpose life; it does the one job.For example: The computer that manages a car engine, a traffic light or a media player, which nobody ever installs software on.
3.2extranet
A private part of the internet, cordoned off from ordinary users, that lets two or more firms do business together. The content is on the web, but only authorized partners can reach it after logging in, and it usually travels through a secured tunnel because the path itself is public.For example: A supplier logging in to a manufacturer’s system to see current orders, confirm shipments and update prices without anyone rekeying the data.
3.2field-programmable gate array (FPGA)
A processor whose circuitry can be reconfigured after it is built, offering customizable hardware acceleration. It sits between a general-purpose processor and a chip designed for a single task.For example: A team that needs one unusual calculation run very fast reshapes the hardware around that calculation instead of buying a chip that will never exist.
3.2file
A block of data that stores specific content, such as a document, an image or a spreadsheet. It is the unit people name, move, share and delete, and it is the reason ordinary users never have to think about where anything physically sits.For example: The report you saved yesterday, which you can find by its name without knowing anything about the disk it is on.
3.2five-nines availability
Availability of 99.999 percent, which works out at just over five minutes of downtime in a year. It is the target data-intensive organizations aim for, and reaching it constrains everything from component design to the choice of site.For example: A payment system that is expected to be unavailable for less time in a whole year than an average lunch break.
3.2folder
A grouping of related files, shown as a folder in a graphical interface and called a directory underneath. Folders nest inside folders, which is how a large amount of digital content stays findable.For example: Keeping coursework in one folder, then a folder per term inside it, then a folder per course inside that.
3.2frameworks and libraries
Collections of prewritten code that developers assemble rather than write. They shorten development time, help one program run on several platforms, and supply the building blocks for specialized work such as machine learning.For example: A small team shipping a working application in weeks because most of what it does was already written by somebody else and is being reused.
3.3generation of computing
Each fundamental change in the way computing technologies work. The usual account runs from vacuum tubes through transistors and integrated circuits to low-cost multimedia machines, widespread internet access, ubiquitous mobile connectivity, and now artificial intelligence and quantum computing.For example: The move from a room-sized machine that a few specialists operated to a phone in everyone’s pocket is several such changes stacked on top of one another.
3.2graphical user interface (GUI)
An interface that lets you instruct a computer by selecting or manipulating pictures, icons and menus rather than by typing commands. It is the reason using a computer no longer requires learning its language first.For example: Dragging a file onto a disk icon instead of typing a copy instruction with the exact path of both places.
3.2graphics processing unit (GPU)
A processor optimized for doing the same operation on very many pieces of data at once, using thousands of small cores. It was built for rendering images, where every pixel can be worked out independently, and turned out to suit machine learning for the same reason.For example: Training a model, where enormous numbers of similar calculations have no need to wait for one another and can all run side by side.
3.4green computing
Using computing resources more efficiently to reduce environmental impact, and using information systems to reduce environmental impact elsewhere. The chapter’s tactics are consolidating underused machines, shifting work to shared providers, managing power on idle desktops, and printing less.For example: Replacing a room of servers that each ran at a fraction of capacity with a few machines doing the same work, and paying less for power and cooling as a result.
3.4grid computing
Combining the computing power of many smaller, independent, networked computers into one system in order to solve a problem that previously needed a supercomputer. Like cloud computing it uses distributed resources, but unlike cloud computing those resources are all applied to a single large problem.For example: A simulation broken into thousands of small pieces, each finished by an ordinary desktop machine somewhere and sent back to be reassembled.
3.2hardware
The physical machines that run the applications and databases an organization needs in order to process transactions and analyze business data. Because organizations perform many different kinds of activity, they need several different kinds of computer to support them.For example: The register at the front of a shop, the server in the back room and the phone in the manager’s pocket are all hardware doing three different jobs.
3.2host name
The part of a web address naming the particular server, or group of servers, that will answer the request. The prefix www usually means the default site, and larger organizations use other host names for their separate services.For example: One organization’s mail service, map service and document storage each answer on a different host name in front of the same domain.
3.2HTML tag
A code set apart with angle brackets that tells a browser how part of a document should be presented, or what that part means. Most tags come in pairs, one to start an element and one to end it.For example: A pair of tags around a phrase can make it bold, mark it as a heading, or turn it into a link to another document.
3.2HTML5
The chapter’s name for the current version of the web’s markup language, which added ways of structuring a page and of presenting modern multimedia without extra software. Treat it as a label for the modern language rather than as a version number still being counted up, because the markup is now revised continuously rather than released in numbered editions.For example: Video that plays in the browser itself, with no separate plug-in to install, because the page can simply say that this is a video.
3.2HTTPS
The secure version of the web’s transfer protocol, now used routinely for anything sensitive because data travelling between a server and a browser can otherwise be intercepted and read. The padlock in the address bar is the browser reporting that it is in use.For example: Entering a card number on a page without the padlock means the number crosses several unknown networks in a form anyone along the way could read.
3.4hybrid cloud
An arrangement in which an organization keeps some applications and data in-house and moves others to a public cloud. The chapter presents it as what organizations usually settle on, because no single provider meets every need and some data is not worth moving.For example: A firm running its public website on rented capacity while its patient records stay on machines it owns and controls.
3.2hyperlink
A reference from one document to another, which the reader can follow. Links are what turn a collection of separate pages into a web rather than a library of unconnected documents.For example: Clicking a word in an article and arriving at the source it was quoting, on a completely different organization’s server.
3.2hypertext
The key feature of the web: documents that contain links to other documents, so a reader can move between them in any order rather than front to back. Everything else about the web is built on top of this one idea.For example: Reading three paragraphs of one page, following a link, and finishing on a page written by somebody who has never heard of the first author.
3.2Hypertext Markup Language (HTML)
The standard method of specifying the structure and content of web pages. It is a text-based format that uses codes called tags to tell the browser what each part of the document is and how it should be presented.For example: Choosing to view the source of any page shows the same words you were reading, wrapped in codes that gave them their headings, links and emphasis.
3.2Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)
